lesson.title: Splitting the Current Path: Inductors in Parallel
lesson.summary: Parallel inductors share the same voltage but split the current between branches, making combined inductance follow the same reciprocal rule as resistors in parallel.
lesson.body:
Wire two inductors so both ends of each one connect to the same pair of nodes, and you have inductors in parallel, sharing the same voltage across every branch at every instant, the same setup you already know from parallel circuits built with resistors. Unlike the series case, where every inductor shared one common current, here each inductor sees the identical voltage V but is free to develop its own current in response, following its own version of V equals L times di over dt rearranged as di over dt equals V divided by L.

The total current flowing into the parallel combination is the sum of whatever current flows into each branch, so the rate of change of the total current is the sum of the individual rates of change: d i-total over dt equals V divided by L1, plus V divided by L2, plus further terms, which factors as V times the quantity 1 divided by L1, plus 1 divided by L2. Comparing that to the defining relationship for the combination as a whole, d i-total over dt equals V divided by L-total, shows that 1 divided by L-total equals 1 divided by L1, plus 1 divided by L2, plus further terms, the same reciprocal, add-the-inverses pattern used for resistors in parallel, and it means the combined inductance of a parallel bank is always smaller than the smallest individual inductor present.

Take the same pair used for the series example, L1 at 10 millihenries and L2 at 15 millihenries, now wired in parallel. Using the reciprocal formula: 1 divided by L-total equals 1 divided by 10, plus 1 divided by 15. With a common denominator of 30, that is 3 divided by 30, plus 2 divided by 30, equal to 5 divided by 30, or 1 divided by 6. So L-total equals 6 millihenries. The faster product-over-sum shortcut for exactly two inductors gives the same result directly: L1 times L2, divided by L1 plus L2, which is 10 times 15, divided by 10 plus 15, or 150 divided by 25, equal to 6 millihenries.

Check that answer against the branch currents directly. Apply 1 volt across the parallel pair. Branch one's current changes at di over dt equals V divided by L1, or 1 divided by 0.01, equal to 100 amps per second. Branch two's current changes at V divided by L2, or 1 divided by 0.015, equal to approximately 66.67 amps per second. Adding the two branch rates gives 100 plus 66.67, or roughly 166.67 amps per second for the total current. Checking against the combined inductance directly, V divided by L-total equals 1 divided by 0.006, which also comes out to approximately 166.67 amps per second, confirming the reciprocal formula.

Just as with resistors in parallel, this reciprocal relationship gives engineers a way to reach an inductance value lower than any single part on hand, and it also shows up in high current power designs, where several inductors are deliberately paralleled across separate windings or separate cores so that the total current is shared among them, easing the heating and saturation limits that a single inductor's wire and core would otherwise face alone. As with the series case, this simple picture assumes the parallel inductors are not magnetically coupled to each other, since coils sharing a magnetic field would need a mutual inductance correction term added to the plain reciprocal formula.
